content: ML Challenge 2026: Business Entity Resolution — Submission Solution
Team Name: NeuralNova
Team Members: Palak Singh; Shivansh Gupta; Rajnish Kumar; Mritunjay Narayan Singh
Submission Date: 27 September 2026
1. Executive Summary
The objective is to identify records that refer to the same real-world business across independent and noisy data sources when no common identifier is available.

The proposed solution uses a scalable hybrid Entity Resolution pipeline: text normalization → multi-key blocking → candidate-pair generation → similarity feature engineering → Random Forest classification → threshold tuning using macro-averaged F0.5 → final entity matches → submission validation.

The key design principle is to avoid all-pairs comparison. Blocking reduces the search space first, while the machine-learning classifier performs the more expensive decision only on plausible candidate pairs.
Because the challenge emphasizes precision through macro-averaged F0.5, the decision threshold is selected on validation data rather than assuming the default probability threshold of 0.50.
2. Problem Analysis
Source	Role
Source 1	Reference business entities
Source 2	Independent records that may correspond to Source 1
Source 3	Another independent source containing potentially matching business records

The training data described in the current solution contains approximately 2.21 million Source-1 records, 5.03 million Source-2 records, and 5.29 million Source-3 records. This scale makes exhaustive pairwise comparison impractical.

Major data-quality issues include capitalization differences, punctuation, spelling errors, abbreviations, word-order changes, transliteration, missing names, missing address components, address formatting differences, and repeated generic business terms.

A Source-1 entity may have zero, one, or multiple corresponding records in another source. Therefore, the solution should not force a one-to-one relationship unless the challenge specification explicitly requires it.

The current solution identifies the training data as containing the US and India and notes France in the test setting. Country is therefore treated as a matching feature/blocking signal rather than being hard-coded as a fixed list.

3. Exploratory Data Analysis
EDA Check	Purpose
Dataset size	Measure scale of each source
Missing values	Understand reliability of name/address fields
Country distribution	Check geographic coverage and consistency
Duplicate analysis	Identify repeated records and potential data-quality issues
Ground-truth match distribution	Understand positive/negative class balance
Data-quality analysis	Identify normalization and blocking requirements
4. Text Normalization
Operation	Purpose
Lowercase conversion	Remove case-based differences
Unicode normalization / transliteration	Reduce representation differences
Replace '&' with 'and'	Normalize common textual variation
Remove punctuation	Reduce formatting noise
Whitespace normalization	Standardize token separation
Apply the same general normalization principles to addresses while preserving meaningful numeric and textual information.
Missing values are handled explicitly. Missing-name and missing-address indicators are retained as features so the classifier can distinguish unavailable information from genuinely dissimilar values.
5. Candidate Generation / Blocking
Blocking is necessary because comparing every Source-1 record with every Source-2 and Source-3 record would create an impractically large search space.
Block 1: normalized business name + country	High-precision candidate path when names are consistent
Block 2: normalized address prefix/block + country	Alternative candidate path when names are noisy or missing

BLOCKING FLOW
Normalized Name + Country
          ↓
   Candidate Set A

Normalized Address Block + Country
          ↓
   Candidate Set B

A ∪ B
 ↓
Remove duplicate candidate pairs
 ↓
Final Candidate Set
Candidate-generation recall is critical: if a true pair is excluded during blocking, no downstream classifier can recover it. Multiple blocking paths reduce dependence on a single noisy field.
The blocking stage should balance recall and computational cost. Blocks that are too strict may lose true matches; blocks that are too broad may create too many candidate pairs.
6. Feature Engineering
Feature Group	Feature	Purpose
Name	WRatio similarity	Measures fuzzy name similarity
Name	Token similarity	Handles token-level ordering and wording differences
Name	Exact normalized-name match	Strong signal when normalized names are identical
Name	Name length difference	Captures structural differences
Name	Name missing indicator	Explicitly represents missing names
Address	WRatio similarity	Measures fuzzy address similarity
Address	Token similarity	Captures overlap between address tokens
Address	Address length difference	Captures structural differences
Address	Address missing indicator	Explicitly represents missing addresses
Geographic	Country match	Checks geographic consistency

Name and address features are complementary. A similar name with a very different address can indicate a false positive, while a slightly different name with a highly similar address can provide evidence for a true match.
7. Matching Model
Model: Random Forest Classifier
Label	Meaning
1	Match
0	Non-match
Configuration	Purpose
Balanced class weighting	Handle class imbalance
Randomized feature selection	Improve tree diversity
Minimum leaf-size regularization	Reduce overfitting
Parallel training	Improve training speed
Random Forest is suitable for mixed, nonlinear similarity features and does not require the feature relationships to be purely linear.
8. Train / Validation Strategy

VALIDATION FLOW
All labeled candidate pairs
          ↓
Split by Source-1 entity ID
          ↓
Training entities          Validation entities
          ↓                       ↓
Model training          Probability prediction
          ↓                       ↓
          Threshold sweep
                 ↓
       Macro F0.5 evaluation
                 ↓
       Select validation threshold

The split is performed at the Source-1 entity level rather than randomly splitting candidate pairs. This reduces information leakage caused by the same underlying entity appearing in both training and validation.
Evaluate a range of probability thresholds on the validation set. Select the threshold that maximizes the challenge-specific macro F0.5 score, subject to the challenge's exact evaluation protocol.
9. Evaluation Metric and Thresholding
F0.5 = (1 + 0.5^2) × Precision × Recall / ((0.5^2 × Precision) + Recall)
F0.5 weights precision more heavily than recall. This makes threshold selection important because accepting too many uncertain matches can reduce the final metric.

Model probability p
       ↓
Try threshold τ1 → calculate macro F0.5
Try threshold τ2 → calculate macro F0.5
Try threshold τ3 → calculate macro F0.5
       ↓
Compare validation scores
       ↓
Select best validated τ
       ↓
Apply τ to test candidates

Do not report an estimated or manually chosen final score. The final precision, recall, F0.5, and selected threshold should be copied from the completed validation notebook after the full pipeline is executed.
10. Error Analysis
False Positive Cause	Why it happens	Mitigation
Similar business names	Different businesses can share generic names	Use address and country similarity jointly
Incomplete addresses	Name may dominate the decision	Use missing indicators and conservative thresholding
Shared generic terms	Words such as Solutions, Services, Consulting, Corporation occur across businesses	Use token and address features
Short names	Short strings contain limited identity information	Require stronger supporting evidence
False Negative Cause	Why it happens	Mitigation
Strongly altered names	Spelling, abbreviations, transliteration reduce similarity	Improve normalization and fuzzy/token features
Noisy addresses	Important address components may be missing or reordered	Use multiple address representations
Missing fields	Fewer signals are available	Retain missing indicators and use alternate blocks
Blocking failure	True pair never reaches classifier	Monitor candidate-generation recall and add complementary blocks
11. Scalability and Efficiency

Naive entity resolution is approximately O(N×M) for two sources. Blocking reduces the comparison workload to the number of generated candidate pairs, making the expensive similarity and model stages substantially more scalable.
Stage	Efficiency Strategy
Normalization	Vectorized/string preprocessing where possible
Blocking	Dictionary/hash-based lookup on blocking keys
Candidate pairs	Deduplicate before feature computation
Features	Compute only for candidate pairs
Model	Parallel Random Forest training/inference
Output	Write compact TSV outputs rather than retaining unnecessary intermediate data in memory
12. End-to-End Algorithm

FOR EACH SOURCE
1. Load records
2. Normalize name and address
3. Create blocking keys
4. Generate candidates
5. Union and deduplicate candidates
6. Compute similarity features
7. Train / load classifier
8. Predict match probability
9. Apply validated threshold
10. Produce entity matches
11. Validate submission schema
12. Save final TSV outputs

for each source record:
    normalize(name, address)
    create(name_country_block)
    create(address_country_block)

candidate_pairs = union(name_block_candidates, address_block_candidates)
candidate_pairs = deduplicate(candidate_pairs)

features = build_features(candidate_pairs)
model.fit(train_features, train_labels)
probabilities = model.predict_proba(test_features)[:, 1]
predictions = probabilities >= validated_threshold

validate_submission(predictions)
write_output_tsv(predictions)

15. Risks and Future Improvements
Risk 1: Overly strict blocking can reduce candidate recall.
Risk 2: Very broad blocks can increase candidate-pair volume and runtime.
Risk 3: Generic business names can produce false positives.
Risk 4: Missing name and address fields reduce available evidence.
Improvement: Add additional blocking keys such as postal-code fragments, phone fragments, website/domain signals, or administrative-region keys when those fields are present in the challenge data.
Improvement: Add character n-gram similarity, Jaro-Winkler, edit distance, numeric-address overlap, and domain-specific token weighting when supported by the data.
Improvement: Compare Random Forest against a calibrated gradient-boosted tree model using the same entity-level validation protocol.
Improvement: Monitor candidate-generation recall separately from classifier recall so blocking failures are not confused with model failures.

Core innovation: combine high-recall multi-key candidate generation with precision-oriented machine-learning matching. This gives a practical balance between large-scale computational efficiency and robust entity matching.
The pipeline is reproducible because preprocessing, candidate generation, feature engineering, training, validation, prediction, and submission validation are separated into explicit stages.
Important submission rule: replace any placeholder validation result with the exact score and threshold produced by the final executed validation notebook. Never submit guessed or estimated metrics.
